message.content: I'm sorry you're in so much pain. I'd like to understand what's going on so I can help quickly. Two questions to start: 1) What kind of catheter do you have (a urinary catheter, a suprapubic catheter, or a drain somewhere else, such as a kidney tube or an abdominal drain), and why was it put in? 2) When did it stop draining, and did the pain and shortness of breath start suddenly at that point? Have you also had fever, swelling of your belly, or not been able to pass urine?

1) It's a catheter that goes into my urine pouch through the stoma on my belly. I was born with spina bifida, and years ago they made my bladder bigger using part of my bowel and gave me a stoma so I could catheterize. Later I had bladder cancer, so they took my bladder out and made me a new pouch for urine, a MAINZ pouch. I normally drain it myself with a catheter. For the past few weeks it's been getting harder and harder to get the catheter in, so they left a catheter in the pouch to drain it all the time.

2) It stopped draining last night, and since then hardly any urine has come out. After that the pain low in my belly came on and it's really bad now, and my breathing has been getting worse and worse. I can't tell you about a fever, nobody has checked. I'm not sure about swelling either.

Thank you, that history helps a lot. Your pouch was made from bowel and can only hold so much. When the catheter stops draining, urine builds up and the pouch can stretch a lot. A very full pouch can push up on your diaphragm and make it harder to breathe. In rare cases, the pouch wall can leak or tear, and urine gets into the belly. That can cause severe pain and make you very unwell. I'd now like to examine you. I'll check your vital signs, including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen levels. I'll also look at your belly, the stoma and the catheter, and listen to your chest.

message.content: The exam shows your heart and lungs are under serious strain, so we need to act quickly. My main concerns are: (1) the pouch has become badly overstretched because the catheter is blocked, or (2) the pouch has leaked or burst and urine has spread into your belly. Either can cause severe pain and trouble breathing. Infection or kidney strain are also possible. I'm ordering urgent blood tests and a CT scan of your belly and pelvis to see the pouch and look for any leak or free fluid. I'm also testing your urine and blood for infection. While we wait, the team will support your breathing and circulation.

message.content:
The CT scan shows what's causing your pain and breathing trouble. The urine pouch has a large tear in its wall on the back left side. Urine has leaked into your belly, and there's fluid around your bowels. The blocked catheter let the pouch overfill, and the pressure made the wall burst. Leaked urine irritates the lining of the belly, which is called peritonitis. That causes the severe pain, puts strain on your heart and lungs, and can lead to serious infection (sepsis).

This is an emergency. You'll need surgery to repair or rebuild the pouch, wash out your belly, and put in drains. After that you'll go to intensive care for support with your breathing and circulation and for antibiotics. Your blood tests show signs of a strong inflammatory reaction. The urine from your pouch later grew a germ called Pseudomonas, so your antibiotics will be chosen to treat it. I'm admitting you now under the urology and surgical teams.
